learn.title: Second Life EV Batteries for Grid Storage
learn.intro: Repurposing retired EV batteries extends their lifespan while reducing waste and costs for grid storage. With global EV sales soaring, managing battery end-of-life is critical for sustainable energy transitions. These batteries offer 70-80% residual capacity after vehicle use, making them affordable alternatives to new storage systems. IRENA's lifecycle analysis highlights their economic viability for renewable energy integration.
learn.c1_text: After 8-10 years in vehicles, EV batteries retain 70-80% capacity. Modules are tested, sorted by health, and repackaged for stationary storage. Like reusing a smartphone battery for a power bank, this extends utility while cutting costs 30-50% versus new systems.
learn.c2_text: These batteries excel at frequency regulation, peak shaving, and renewable smoothing. A typical 60kWh module can power 5 homes for 4 hours. Their modular design allows scalable deployment, crucial for integrating intermittent solar/wind into grids needing rapid response balancing.
learn.c3_text: India's 1.5 million EV sales in 2023 signal future battery demand. MNRE aims to establish 500 GWh grid storage by 2030. Repurposing EV batteries could supply 20% of this, with startups like SunEnergy India piloting second-life projects in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.

learn.title: Pumped Hydro Storage: Earth's Largest Battery
learn.intro: Pumped hydro storage dominates global grid flexibility with 94% of installed energy storage capacity. By moving water between reservoirs, it provides reliable long-duration storage for renewable energy. As wind and solar penetrate grids, this technology remains irreplaceable for balancing supply-demand gaps over hours to days. IRENA's innovation outlook confirms its role as backbone infrastructure.
learn.c1_text: Excess electricity powers pumps moving water uphill to an upper reservoir (charging). During demand peaks, water flows downhill through turbines to generate power (discharging). Like a gravity battery, a 1,000MW plant can store 24GWh—enough to power 2 million homes for 24 hours.
learn.c2_text: Round-trip efficiency reaches 70-85%, with round-trip losses minimal. Requires specific topography: two water bodies separated by 300-500m elevation. Modern projects use modular dam designs and closed-loop systems to minimize environmental impact, suitable for decommissioned mines or quarries.
learn.c3_text: India's 1,200GW hydro potential includes 50GW economically viable. Recent projects like Nathpa Jhakri (1.5GW) and proposed 10GW pumped storage aim to support 500GW renewable target by 2030. States like Himachal Pradesh prioritize these for green energy corridors linking solar/wind regions.

learn.title: Flow Batteries: Vanadium & Iron Systems
learn.intro: Flow batteries revolutionize grid storage by decoupling energy and power. Liquid electrolytes in tanks store energy chemically, enabling rapid scaling and 20+ year lifespans. Vanadium and iron-based systems offer safety, recyclability, and long-duration discharge—critical for multi-hour renewable integration. The US DOE emphasizes their role in decarbonizing heavy industry and microgrids.
learn.c1_text: Two electrolyte liquids (e.g., vanadium sulfate) flow through a membrane, generating current via redox reactions. Energy capacity scales with tank size—doubling tanks doubles storage. Unlike lithium-ion, they don't degrade structurally. A 100kWh system uses 1,000L of electrolyte, ideal for remote solar farms needing 4-8 hour backup.
learn.c2_text: Vanadium systems offer high energy density (25-35Wh/kg) and stability but cost $300-500/kWh. Iron-based alternatives use cheaper, abundant materials ($150-200/kWh) with lower voltage (1.6V vs 1.2V). Both enable 10,000+ cycles, but vanadium excels in temperature tolerance (-5°C to 50°C), while iron suits warmer climates.
learn.c3_text: India's Department of Science collaborates with IITs on vanadium R&D, targeting $200/kWh by 2030. NTPC's 10MWh pilot in Gujarat tests flow tech for solar smoothing. With 500km2 suitable land for storage, India's 500GW renewable target demands cost-effective long-duration solutions like these.

learn.title: Lithium-Ion Battery Storage: Grid Applications
learn.intro: Lithium-ion batteries dominate grid storage with 90% market share due to high energy density, fast response, and falling costs. They enable renewable integration, peak shaving, and microgrid resilience. The US DOE highlights their role in transforming grids, with applications from residential storage to utility-scale projects. Understanding their operation and limitations is key for energy transition strategies.
learn.c1_text: During charging, lithium ions move from cathode to anode via electrolyte, storing energy as chemical potential. Discharging reverses this flow, releasing electrons through external circuits to power devices. A 100kWh home battery uses graphite anodes and lithium iron phosphate cathodes, lasting 10-15 years with 5,000-7,000 cycles at 80% retention.
learn.c2_text: Li-ion systems provide milliseconds response for frequency regulation, 4-hour peak shaving, and solar/wind smoothing. Round-trip efficiency hits 85-90%, outperforming pumped hydro's 70-85%. Their modular design enables rapid deployment—Tesla's Hornsdale Power Reserve (150MW) stabilized Australia's grid after coal closures.
learn.c3_text: India's 2023 policy targets 500MWh grid storage by 2025. Projects like Tata Power's 10MWh in Mumbai use Li-ion for residential backup. With 7.5GW solar auctions, these batteries optimize rooftop solar economics via time-of-use arbitrage. Government subsidies under PM-KUSUM aim for 10GWh storage by 2030.

learn.title: Rooftop Solar & Net Metering in India
learn.intro: Rooftop solar democratizes energy access by enabling distributed generation, reducing transmission losses, and empowering consumers. India's net metering policies allow surplus power sale to grids, improving affordability. With solar tariffs at $0.026/kWh, rooftop systems are increasingly viable for households and businesses, aligning with the nation's 500GW renewable ambition by 2030.
learn.c1_text: Solar panels convert sunlight to DC electricity via photovoltaics. An inverter transforms DC to AC for home use. Excess power flows to the grid through a bi-directional meter. A 1kW system generates 4-5kWh daily, meeting 30-40% of average Indian household consumption. Net metering credits surplus production at retail rates.
learn.c2_text: MNRE's 2023 guidelines mandate utilities to buy surplus power at same tariff consumers pay. Net metering applies up to 1MW for businesses, with 1:1 credit ratio. States like Gujarat offer 6% capital subsidy under KUSUM, while Maharashtra allows 15-year agreements. Rooftop capacity reached 7.5GW in 2023, targeting 100GW by 2030.
learn.c3_text: India's 2023 target of 100GW rooftop solar faces challenges like complex approvals and land scarcity. Rewa Solar Park's 500MW project showcases utility-scale success. With 300,000 subsidy beneficiaries under KUSUM Phase I, rooftop systems reduce urban grid strain. Tamil Nadu's net metering portal processed 2,000 applications monthly in 2023.

learn.title: Bifacial Solar Panels: Dual-Side Generation
learn.intro: Bifacial panels capture sunlight from both sides, boosting energy yield by 10-30% through rear-side albedo effects. As costs fall, they're reshaping utility-scale solar with higher output per square meter. IRENA highlights their potential to cut LCOE while minimizing land use. Understanding their technology and optimal deployment is vital for maximizing renewable energy returns.
learn.c1_text: Transparent backsheet or glass allows light absorption from ground reflection (albedo). White surfaces reflect 20-90% light back, adding 10-25% more power. A 400W monofacial panel becomes 440W bifacial equivalent. Concentrated in snowy regions (80% albedo) or white gravel sites, gains exceed 30% annually.
learn.c2_text: Optimal tilt angles (10-20°) maximize rear exposure. Elevated mounting (1-2m) ensures ground reflection. IRENA studies show 15% annual yield increase in desert climates. Temperature coefficients improve too—bifacial panels run 2-3°C cooler, enhancing efficiency in hot regions like Rajasthan or Andhra Pradesh.
learn.c3_text: India's 2023 solar auctions favor bifacial tech for 100GW capacity. NTPC's 100MW Kurnool project uses bifacial panels on white gravel, achieving 22% yield boost. With 300 sunny days/year, India's high DNI (1,500-2,000kWh/m²) suits bifacial deployment. MNRE subsidizes 30% cost increase, targeting 50GW bifacial by 2030 for green hydrogen production.
